take_homes: Two kinds of check: one stops the agent making stuff up, the other pushes the output to be actually useful. We only have the first kind.
A flat or perfect score means the judge ran out of things to find. It does not mean the work is good, and nobody has checked the judge against human verdicts.
My job is to design the loop and own what good means, and also to keep reading some real output myself.

monday.move: Take our code review rubric as the judge and put it in the generate/judge/rewrite-tactic loop for one engineering agent. Then score about ten outputs by hand next to the judge.
monday.who: Me and one senior engineer. The sales-team setup is not happening.
monday.when: Monday morning for the loop; the hand-scoring comparison Wednesday.
monday.stop_condition: If the judge and our hand scores disagree on more than about 2 in 10, we fix the judge before trusting any score.
monday.blocker: Nobody outside engineering has asked for this. I haven't decided who owns the judge file. I'll probably skip the manual check if I'm busy.

misconception.why: I thought a good agent means good output and checking is for beginners. The line that a generator grading itself passes itself, plus the point that a clean score hides the judge's blind spots, made me see my 'it looked fine' skipping as the same thing. I'm not fully converted: I skipped the SHA check and the manual read in the session, and I'd likely skip them again unless forced.

one_line: Good for how to run agents without babysitting them, and the 'who checks the judge' part stung a bit. The first half is slow for anyone already running agents.
